whys: Best available summary of how subs break through ice

comments.author: ortusdux
comments.story: Metallurgist admits faking steel test results for US Navy subs
comments.why: Best available summary of how subs break through ice
comments.text: The Navy is understandably cagey about how they surface through ice-sheets, but this Smarter Every Day video is the best summary I have seen. [VIDEO] Basically, some part of the sub needs to be strong enough to reliably break ice at sub-zero temps. The rest needs to maintain its strength at those temps.

comments.author: dataviz1000
comments.story: Submarine missing near Titanic used a $30 Logitech gamepad for steering
comments.why: Shows mechanical ballast and throttle controls on an Ohio class sub
comments.text: The YouTube channel SmarterEveryDay was invited to film on an Ohio class nuclear submarine training in the Arctic. [0] You can see how many of the system are mechanical and not electronic in the demonstration especially the ballast controls. Most if not all boats and ships can control the throttle mechanically so if the boat loses its electronics such as a wave smashing the windshield in, it is still possible to control the rudder and throttles. I was very surprised at the lack if mechanical controls on the recreational submarine. [0] [VIDEO]

comments.author: paranoidrobot
comments.story: USS Connecticut (SSN 22) struck an object while submerged on Oct. 2
comments.why: Shows upward-looking cameras on a submarine surfacing through ice
comments.text: They have upward-looking cameras, at least on some of them. You can see it in the last Smarter Every Day video[1] where they're talking about surfacing a submarine in the arctic ocean. At several points you can see a video monitor showing an upward view of the ice. [1] [VIDEO] e: to be clear, that upward looking camera isn't going to be enough to detect much beyond your own footprint. If someone is about to cross that area you'd need some other way of detecting them.
